On simplicity

Posted on April 12, 2026 by someone

Software engineers reach for complexity too fast. This post argues we should reach for it more slowly, and that the cost of doing so is rarely what we think it is.

The myth of the generic abstraction

You open a file. You write five lines. They work. Then someone on the team says “we should make this generic” and suddenly you have a builder pattern, three traits, and a factory.

fn hello() -> String {
    String::from("hi")
}

The generic version is not an improvement. The generic version is a bet on a future that has not arrived. That bet costs every reader for the rest of the file’s life.

The cheapest code is code that doesn’t exist. The second cheapest is code a junior can delete without fear.

When abstraction is worth it

Abstraction pays when three conditions hold:

  1. You have three concrete uses — not one, not two.
  2. Those uses change together under realistic pressures.
  3. The abstraction boundary compresses the mental model, rather than expanding it.

If any of those conditions fails, you’re paying interest on a loan for a purchase you never make.

What to do instead

Write the concrete version. Ship it. Observe what actually changes. Then, if a pattern emerges, refactor with the benefit of evidence. See also: YAGNI, the rule of three.
